analysis.one_liner: Replaces EPA permitting of ship discharges with uniform Coast Guard ballast-water standards and preempts stricter state rules.
analysis.headline: The Senate Commerce Committee approved the bill on a bipartisan basis and put it on the Senate calendar, but it never received a floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Ships routinely discharge ballast water and other operational wastewater, which can carry invasive species and pollutants into U.S. waters. This bill would move regulation of those discharges from the EPA's Clean Water Act permitting system to a single set of national standards written by the Coast Guard, and would bar states from enforcing their own stricter rules except through a narrow petition to the federal government. It also would mandate tighter numeric ballast-water limits by 2022, require saltwater flushing before oceangoing ships enter the Great Lakes, and permanently exempt small vessels from permitting.
analysis.who_benefits: Shipping companies and vessel owners would get one national set of rules instead of a patchwork of state standards and EPA permits, plus a process to win compliance extensions. Manufacturers of ballast-water treatment equipment would gain a government-certified market, since every covered vessel would need certified technology. Small commercial vessels, fishing vessels, and recreational boats would be permanently exempt from federal discharge permits.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would make Coast Guard national standards the exclusive federal authority for vessel discharges, superseding any other permitting requirement or prohibition [S3] [S4].

It would keep the Coast Guard's 2012 ballast-water rule in place and require a final rule by January 1, 2022 adopting stricter numeric discharge limits, unless a feasibility review finds the standard unattainable [S3] [S4].

It would require vessels entering the Great Lakes from outside U.S. waters through the St. Lawrence River to saltwater-flush all ballast tanks before entry, a safeguard against invasive species [S3] [S4].
It would create a Coast Guard certification system for ballast-water treatment technology, with EPA-issued testing protocols and a bar on technologies using certain biocides [S3] [S4].
The reported version would make permanent a moratorium on discharge permits for small vessels that was otherwise set to expire in December 2017 [S3].

analysis.who_pays: State governments would lose the power to set and enforce stricter ballast-water rules for their own waters; they could keep stricter standards only if the federal government approved a petition showing the technology exists and the rules meet international obligations. Coastal and Great Lakes waters would bear whatever risk remains where federal standards lag behind the rules states would have set. Shippers would pay for treatment systems and compliance, costs likely passed through freight rates.

drawbacks.text: The bill would prohibit states from adopting or enforcing any statute or regulation on vessel discharges after enactment, overturning the framework where states could act alongside federal permits [S4].

A state could enforce a stricter ballast standard only if the Coast Guard approved its petition, with determinations required within 90 days and strict showing requirements on feasibility, technology availability, and international consistency [S4].
Vessel owners could petition for compliance-deadline extensions of up to 18 months renewable once more, and a petition would be deemed approved if the Coast Guard did not act within 90 days [S4].

The bill would permanently exempt small commercial vessels, fishing vessels, and recreational vessels from discharge permits, and exempt geographically limited operations from ballast standards [S3] [S4].

Even the stricter 2022 standard is conditional: if no certified technology can meet it, the Coast Guard would instead require only the best technology available, and installed systems could keep operating through their service life even after standards tighten [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers a real gain: one enforceable national standard, a mandated tightening by 2022, and a Great Lakes flushing rule. But it buys that by taking away state authority and replacing Clean Water Act permitting, so waters in stricter states would be protected only as strongly as the federal standard, and only as fast as the Coast Guard and EPA write rules. How good the trade is would depend heavily on whether regulators met their deadlines and whether the feasibility review allowed the stricter standard to take effect.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Commerce Committee approved the bill and put it on the Senate calendar in July 2015, but no floor vote was ever scheduled before the Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Sen. Marco Rubio introduced the bill on February 4, 2015, joined by a bipartisan group of cosponsors, and it was referred to the Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee [S1] [S5] [S6].
The committee ordered the bill reported favorably on February 26, 2015, and reported it on July 29, 2015 with an amendment in the nature of a substitute [S6].
The same day, the bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 171, where it remained [S4] [S6].
No further action was taken; the 114th Congress ended January 3, 2017 without the Senate voting on the bill [S1] [S6].
Twenty-seven senators cosponsored the bill, 19 Republicans and 8 Democrats, including the Commerce Committee chairman and senators from both coastal and interior states [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, existing law stayed in place: states kept their ability to regulate ship discharges and EPA permitting continued. Shipping operators did not get the single national standard and preemption of state rules they had sought, and stronger federal ballast limits were not enacted in that Congress.

for.name: Ocean shipping and cruise industries
for.what_they_did: Backed a single national discharge standard to replace the state-by-state patchwork and EPA permitting.

against.name: Environmental and Great Lakes conservation groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill as a rollback of Clean Water Act protections and a preemption of state authority over ballast water.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan from the start: 27 cosponsors split 19 Republicans and 8 Democrats, and the committee reported the bill favorably without a recorded opposition vote.

industries.note: The bill would replace EPA Clean Water Act permits and a patchwork of state rules with one Coast Guard-written national standard, and would bar states from enforcing stricter rules without federal approval. Shippers gain regulatory certainty and lower compliance friction; the cost is weaker protection for the public waters ships discharge into, especially where states had set tougher standards.

Every covered vessel would need Coast Guard-certified treatment technology, with EPA-issued testing protocols, creating a guaranteed market for these systems. Their product's success runs alongside cleaner waters, though foreign-certified systems and grandfathering of installed equipment could soften the demand they receive.

industries.industry: Small commercial vessels, fishing fleets, and recreational boating
industries.note: The reported bill would make permanent a moratorium on discharge permits for small vessels and exempt fishing and recreational vessels outright, lifting a regulatory burden. Those same discharges would go unregulated, so nearby waters bear the difference.
